Minor Hotels to manage Gardens of Eden resort in Phuket, slated to open in 2031
article:
Thailand-based hospitality operator Minor Hotels has signed a hotel management agreement with Amal Group of Companies for Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket. This marks the first property under its Minor Reserve Collection luxury brand in Asia.

Scheduled to open in 2031, the resort will be located in Bang Tao, Phuket, comprising a 100-key hotel and 210 one- to three-bedroom residences. It will form the hospitality centrepiece of Gardens of Eden, a 33-acre integrated luxury living and wellness development by Amal Group that will also comprise Etro Residences and Gardens of Eden Residences.

The resort will feature a wellness facility spanning more than 53,820 sq ft. Guests will also have access to a range of dining options, including an all-day dining restaurant, two specialty restaurants, an organic café and a lobby lounge.

“Thailand is home for Minor Hotels, so introducing the new Gardens of Eden Phuket, Minor Reserve Collection to the kingdom is a significant milestone for our company and our luxury brand strategy,” said Omar Romero, chief development and luxury officer, Minor Hotels.

Alexander Chuvalov, CEO of Gardens of Eden, added: “Phuket remains one of the world's most attractive resort markets, and we believe the combination of Minor Hotels' luxury hospitality expertise and the strength of the Gardens of Eden vision will create a distinctive offering for both international travellers and residents.”

Gardens of Eden Resort Phuket will join a growing global portfolio of Minor Reserve Collection properties, which includes 640 hotels, resorts and branded residences across 67 countries.

title: Is Now a Good Time to Buy Stocks?
article:
“Should I buy stocks now or wait for the market to fall further?”
This is a question many investors find themselves asking after periods of market volatility.
Buying too early and watching prices continue to fall can make some uneasy.
But waiting too long might mean missing a market recovery.
Why Investors Are Hesitating to Buy Stocks
The
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) had a great start this year.
It climbed steadily and reached a record of 5,801.96 on 4 September 2026.
Lately, however, it has been pulling back.
The STI has since fallen 8.6% from its record high, dropping to 5,303.82 on 2 November 2026.
Investors are becoming more cautious as uncertainty surrounding interest rates, economic growth and
geopolitical tensions
influences global markets.
Negative headlines can weaken investor confidence, and investors worry about buying just before a downturn.
When prices fall immediately following a purchase, investors may regret it, which prompts them to wait until market conditions appear more stable before buying again.
Waiting for that “perfect” price is challenging because markets are unpredictable.
Hesitating too long may lead to missed opportunities.
Three Reasons to Consider Buying Stocks Now
1. Market declines can create attractive valuations
Falling share prices can present opportunities to buy quality companies at more reasonable valuations.
The share price of
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) fell by approximately 16% in early April 2025.
This occurred despite DBS reporting a record net profit of S$11.4 billion for FY2024, an 11% year-on-year increase.
Investors should note that the market sell-off was primarily driven by macroeconomic conditions, including US tariff announcements, as well as a scheduled ex-dividend date on 7 April, rather than issues with the underlying business.
Look beyond share prices and analyse the company’s price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, cash flow and long-term growth prospects.
2. Time in the market matters more than timing the market
Staying invested
allows investors to enjoy growth and better returns as a result of compounding.
Investors who bought DBS shares just before the dip in April 2025 and held them until 30 October 2026 would have seen a nearly 60% capital gain.
Shares purchased on 1 April 2025 at S$45.62 each were worth S$73.13 on 30 October 2026.
3. Dividend investors can benefit from lower entry prices
If a company continues paying the same annual dividend while its share price declines, investors purchasing at the lower price receive a higher yield relative to their investment.
However, investors should prioritise dividend sustainability by assessing a company’s earnings, cash flow and payout ratio rather than being attracted solely to a high headline yield.
Three Reasons Why Waiting Might Make Sense
1. Stock valuations may still be expensive
A market decline does not automatically mean that stocks are cheap.
Investors should assess valuations using the P/E ratio and the price-to-book (P/B) ratio.
They should also consider future earnings expectations, as overly optimistic forecasts may already be reflected in share prices.
2. Corporate earnings could deteriorate
Slower economic growth, weaker consumer demand and rising operating costs can reduce profitability.
Find out whether the falling share prices reflect temporary market weakness or deeper structural problems.
3. Your financial circumstances may not support investing yet
Rather than asking “should I invest now?”, ask whether you can afford to.
Money required within the next few years for essential commitments is unsuitable for stock market investments since markets can experience significant fluctuations and may not recover in time when funds are needed.
Having a stable financial foundation helps investors avoid being forced to sell shares at unfavourable prices.
Buy Now or Wait: What Does History Tell Us?
Stock markets can recover surprisingly quickly after sharp declines.
The S&P 500 plunged approximately 34% from its February 2020 peak of 3,386.15 during the COVID-19 sell-off in March 2020.
However, on 18 August 2020, despite the ongoing pandemic, the index pushed past the February record to close at 3,389.78.
Investors who waited for complete certainty before returning to the market risked missing a significant portion of the rebound.
Still, neither buying now nor waiting guarantees better results, as the outcome depends on market movements and investment timing.
A Smarter Approach: Invest Gradually Instead of Guessing the Bottom
Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) involves investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, regardless of market movements.
The same investment amount buys more shares when share prices decrease.
This approach reduces the need to find an ideal time to buy, although it does not ensure profits.
Maintaining a cash reserve enables you to take advantage of opportunities during market declines.
Investors who have cash reserves can purchase shares when high-quality companies experience temporary price drops.
However, holding excessive cash indefinitely while waiting for the perfect buying opportunity can result in missed market gains.
Rather than attempting to predict short-term price movements, investors should prioritise quality companies with strong balance sheets.
Businesses with manageable debt, established competitive advantages and reliable earnings are better positioned to navigate economic uncertainty and downturns.
That said, even a financially strong company can be a poor investment if purchased at an excessive valuation.
What Should Singapore Investors Do Today?
Long-term investors may benefit from starting or continuing to invest during periods of market uncertainty.
Exchange-traded funds (ETFs)
reduce reliance on individual stocks, providing exposure to a broad range of holdings.
Investors could consider adding established Singapore blue chips, such as DBS and
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), better known as Singtel, as part of a diversified portfolio.
Income investors must assess whether companies can sustain their payouts over the long term.
Important indicators include payout ratios, operating cash flow, earnings consistency and debt levels.
A market correction may create opportunities to accumulate shares in established dividend-paying companies at lower prices.
Be cautious of unusually high yields, as these may reflect falling share prices or business health concerns.
Beginners or those uncomfortable with volatility may prefer a gradual investment approach with DCA.
DCA helps reduce the emotional pressure associated with market timing while allowing beginners to gain experience and confidence over time.
Diversification across different sectors and geographical markets is also important to reduce individual company risks.
Get Smart: Don’t Wait for the Perfect Moment
Rather than asking “is now a good time to buy stocks?”, ask whether your financial circumstances, investment objectives and the current market valuations support investing now.
Market declines can create opportunities, but not every falling stock is good value.
Investing gradually in quality businesses with DCA may be more practical than trying to predict the next market movement.

title: DBS, Singtel or Microsoft: 3 Very Different Stocks for a Long-Term Portfolio
article:
The best stock for a
long-term portfolio
isn’t always the one with the best share price run.
So, what should you look for, and could one portfolio hold three very different companies?
DBS Group Holdings Ltd
(SGX: D05) is Singapore’s biggest bank.
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, runs telcos here and in Australia, and owns stakes in phone companies around the region.
Microsoft Corporation
(NASDAQ: MSFT) is the US software giant behind Windows and the Azure cloud.
They do quite different jobs in a portfolio.
DBS and Singtel are mainly there for the dividends, while you’d own Microsoft for growth.
DBS: A Dividend-Paying Banking Powerhouse
Start with the one that is a favourite among Singapore investors.
DBS
has operations spread across Asia, and it is very good at making money.
In its latest results, for the first half of 2026 (1H2026), the bank earned a record net profit of S$6.01 billion.
Crucially, this was achieved with a stunning return on equity (ROE) of 17.9%, which is the best among the three local banks.
DBS’s wealth management business helped, with fees from affluent clients hitting a record S$1.83 billion.
That money flowed back to shareholders.
Over the last twelve months (LTM), DBS returned S$3.18 per share in dividends to shareholders (of which S$0.60 per share was a capital return, with the rest being ordinary dividends).
That works out to a trailing yield of 4.3%.
DBS can afford it.
Its capital cushion, the common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio, is healthy at 14.6%. and only 1.0% of its loans have gone bad.
Falling interest rates are the main risk for DBS investors.
Banks earn less on the loans they disburse when rates decline.
DBS is not immune to this, although loan growth and fee income from areas such as wealth management can help cushion the impact.
Slower loan growth and rising credit costs could also weigh on the bank’s earnings.
The key takeaway is that DBS is a fine choice if you’re seeking dividends from an established bank, as long as you accept the interest-rate and economic risks that accompany it.
Singtel: A Combination of Dividends and Regional Growth
Singtel is a different animal.
People keep paying phone and internet bills whatever the economy does, and that steady stream is what the company is built on.
It runs telcos in Singapore and Australia (the latter through Optus).
Ownership stakes in telcos across the region, such as Airtel in India and AIS in Thailand, provide further geographical diversification.
For the financial year ended 31 March 2026 (FY2026), Singtel generated S$2.44 billion in free cash flow.
In the three months to 30 June 2026 (1QFY2027), Singtel’s regional stakes earned S$543 million in profit after tax, up 16% year on year (YoY).
Its data centre arm, Digital InfraCo, grew its top line by 19%, and Optus lifted its EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) by 14%.
Consequently, Singtel’s underlying profit rose 21% from a year ago to S$831 million.
The dividend needs a careful read.
Singtel paid S$0.185 per share for FY2026, but only S$0.134 per share was a regular dividend.
The other S$0.051 came from selling assets, something that can’t go on forever.
Singtel still has about S$2.25 billion in planned asset disposals to complete, after which the additional payout might cease.
At current prices, this translates to a dividend yield of 4.5%.
The risks for the telco giant include intensifying competition for its telco operations and capital expenditure needed to grow its data centre business.
Currency swings are something to pay attention to as well.
On balance, Singtel gives you steady telco cash flow and a slice of the digitalisation and data centre boom.
However, as noted above, its extra dividend payout could be curtailed once its asset disposal programme runs its course.
Microsoft: A Global Technology Growth Engine
Microsoft is the odd one out.
It pays a dividend, but investors buy it for growth.
Much of its revenue recurs.
Businesses pay for Microsoft 365 through subscriptions, while Azure, its cloud platform, bills them for what they actually use.
Microsoft says what sets Azure apart is the hybrid cloud architecture, which lets companies run their own servers alongside it.
Artificial intelligence
(AI) has given Azure a real push.
In the first quarter of its FY2027 (1QFY2027), Azure revenue grew 48% YoY, while total revenue rose 19% YoY to US$92.3 billion.
The catch is how much Microsoft is spending to keep up.
It put US$115.9 billion into property and equipment in FY2026, and it hasn’t slowed down since.
Capital spending hit US$46 billion in 1QFY2027, which knocked free cash flow down to US$18.6 billion.
Shareholders weren’t left out, though.
Microsoft still handed back US$10.2 billion through dividends and buybacks in the quarter, and the hope is that all this spending shows up as bigger profits a few years from now.
You do pay for that growth.
Microsoft trades at about 27 times forward earnings.
The dividend was recently raised 8% to US$0.98 a quarter, but that still only works out to a yield of about 0.75%.
This valuation leaves little room for error, given strong competition from rival cloud providers and AI model makers.
Microsoft may appeal to investors prioritising long-term capital appreciation, although its relatively low dividend yield makes it less suitable for those seeking substantial immediate income.
Should You Own All Three in One Portfolio?
You could, and the mix makes sense.
Banks, telcos and tech companies tend to behave differently.
DBS and Singtel provide reliable dividend income (reinvesting payments received can further turbocharge your compounding journey), while Microsoft provides a stronger growth angle for the portfolio.
But three stocks alone aren’t a portfolio.
Both DBS and Singtel depend heavily on the region, so if the region slows down, you’d feel it in both at once.
Microsoft brings a different problem: it earns in US dollars, leaving you exposed to currency swings.
It’s better to see these three as a starting point, not your whole portfolio.
Get Smart: Different Stocks, Different Roles
So which stock should you pick?
That is the wrong question.
Instead, ask what your portfolio is missing.
If you need income, DBS and Singtel do the heavy lifting.
If you want growth, Microsoft is the one.
Each does a different job, and a good portfolio needs more than one of them.

title: Get Smart: As the STI Dips, is it Time to Buy?
article:
We get plenty of questions at The Smart Investor.
But there’s one that comes up most often:
“What stock should I buy?”
Right now, it’s a question that’s likely on the minds of many investors.
As of last Friday, 23 October 2026, the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI) was down 7% from its 52-week high.
It’s not quite a market correction — that would be a decline of 10% or more.
But after a bull run, the stock market is starting to get bargain hunters interested again.
Especially if you’ve got money set aside.
But here’s the thing: before you ask what to buy, there’s a more important question …
… what stock do you NEED?
You see, different investors have different needs.
And different stocks play different roles.
Ask a stock to do a job it wasn’t built for, and you’re setting yourself up for disappointment.
Picture a pyramid
At The Smart Investor, we like to view a dividend portfolio as a pyramid.
Take a moment to picture one in your head.
At the bottom, where it’s widest, you want a strong foundation.
These are your workhorses — companies or REITs that turn up every quarter or every six months to deliver steady, reliable dividends.
They don’t offer a lot of growth.
But they are reliable.
My colleague, David Kuo, calls them Income Stocks.
Only when you have that stable base do you start layering on growth.
These are your Growth Stocks.
The middle of the pyramid is a designated area for stocks that have the ability to grow their sales and profits — so that they can pay you higher dividends in the future.
Finally, at the very tip, the smallest part of the pyramid, is what I call your testing ground.
This is your speculative space, where you let yourself run a little.
Let me show you what I mean with two Singapore stocks.
The base: the REIT that turns up
First up,
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT.
The REIT owns popular malls and offices, mostly in Singapore.
It’s not flashy. It won’t make headlines.
So what makes it special?
CICT is one of a handful of REITs that have increased their distribution per unit (DPU) — the REIT version of a dividend per share — since 2021.
That may not sound spectacular.
Until you consider what has happened since.
We had the steepest interest rate hikes in decades.
We had Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs.
We had the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Through it all, CICT’s DPU has inched up every year since 2021 like clockwork.
That’s exactly what you want at the bottom of your pyramid: a REIT that turns up, pays you, and doesn’t need you to think about it.
Just don’t expect fireworks.
Expecting 20% growth out of CICT is a bridge too far.
The middle: simple, but not easy
One level up, we have supermarket operator
Sheng Siong
(SGX: OV8).
The best way to describe Sheng Siong’s business?
Simple, but not easy.
Everyone’s been to a Sheng Siong before.
The business is easy to understand.
But it’s really, really hard to do.
Its secret?
In my eyes, Sheng Siong does the simple things really, really well.
For starters, the supermarket operator keeps adding new stores — from 27 at its IPO in 2011 to 90 today.
And it uses money from its existing operations to fund the new store buildout, not debt.
At the same time, it has made its stores more profitable.
Fresh food and house brands play a big part here, made possible by its Mandai distribution centre, which allowed Sheng Siong to cut out the middleman and buy directly from the source.
In short: more stores, and better stores.
It sounds easy. It isn’t.
To be sure, there are risks to watch.
Sheng Siong is building a hefty new warehouse in Sungei Kadut, which could limit the cash available for dividends.
And with the Johor Bahru-Singapore RTS Link on the way, nobody knows how our grocery habits will change until the rubber hits the road.
That’s the trade-off in the middle of the pyramid: a little more uncertainty, in exchange for a business that can grow.
The tip: keep it small
Now for the fun part.
The tip is the most exciting part of the pyramid.
It’s where the big stories live, and it’s tempting to let it grow.
The base, on the other hand, can feel dull.
When a hot stock is flying, a REIT quietly paying its dividends won’t exactly get your pulse racing.
But think about what happens when the tip gets too big.
The whole pyramid becomes unbalanced.
That’s why the testing ground is a controlled area — and you want to be strict about it.
In practice, it comes down to how much you put into each stock.
Bigger positions for the workhorses at the base.
Smaller ones for the ideas at the tip.
That way, if a testing-ground idea doesn’t work out, it stings.
But your foundation holds.
Get Smart: Give every stock a job
So, as you draw up your shopping list during this dip, pause before asking “what stock should I buy?”
Ask what your portfolio needs instead.
If your base is shaky, you probably need a reliable workhorse, not the next big thing.
If your base is solid, you have room to add some growth.
And if you want to scratch that speculative itch, do it at the tip.
Again, keep it small.
Plainly speaking, before you give a stock your money, give it a job.
That’s how we think about dividend investing at The Smart Investor.

title: Ahead of UOB’s Earnings: 3 Key Metrics Investors Must Watch
article:
Profit went up. The total income fell.
That gap sums up the first half of 2026 for
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11).
Net profit grew because UOB set aside less money for bad loans, not because the business earned more.
On 4 November 2026, the bank will report its third-quarter earnings — the first of the
big three
to do so.
That’s when investors will find out if the core engine has started to turn.
For context, UOB operates across 19 countries and territories, with Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Greater China as its core markets.
Today, it serves more than 8.5 million retail customers across ASEAN.
For the first half ended 30 June 2026, UOB’s total income slipped 1% year on year to S$7.0 billion.
Operating profit before allowances fell 4% to S$3.9 billion.
Net profit attributable to shareholders still rose 3% to S$2.9 billion.
The reason?
Total allowances dropped 27% to S$414 million.
In other words, lower provisions propped up the bottom line.
UOB cannot keep cutting allowances forever.
For dividends to keep rising, income has to start growing again.
So what should you look for on 4 November?
Start with these three numbers.
The first-half figures below set the yardstick.
Metric
1H’26
Year-ago comparison
Net interest margin (NIM)
1.78%
1.96%
Gross customer loans
S$361.4 billion

Non-interest income
S$2.4 billion

Figures are for the six months ended 30 June 2026. Source: UOB.
Has the margin squeeze run its course?
Net interest margin, or NIM, tells you how much a bank earns on its loans after paying for its funding.
As benchmark rates fell, UOB’s NIM narrowed to 1.78% in the first half from 1.96% a year ago.
Net interest income dropped 3% to S$4.6 billion.
Net interest income makes up about two-thirds of UOB’s total income.
So even a small shift in the margin goes a long way.
On 4 November, watch which way NIM moves.
If the margin holds near first-half levels, the worst of the rate cuts may have passed.
If it falls sharply again, loans and fees will have more ground to make up.
Can loan growth keep filling the gap?
When margins shrink, a bank can make up some of the shortfall by lending more.
UOB did just that.
Gross customer loans grew 5% year on year to S$361.4 billion.
The extra lending softened the blow to net interest income, though it couldn’t fully offset it.
More loans only help if borrowers pay them back.
UOB’s non-performing loans (NPL) ratio held unchanged at 1.6%, so asset quality has stayed steady.
For the third quarter, you’ll want to see loans keep growing at a similar pace while the NPL ratio stays put.
Will wealth fees take over from interest income?
Non-interest income rose 1% year on year to S$2.4 billion.
That headline number hides two very different stories.
Wealth management fees climbed 15% to S$462 million.
Loan-related fees went the other way and fell 19% to S$347 million.
The slide in loan fees outweighed the wealth gains, and net fee and commission income dipped 2% to S$1.3 billion.
Other non-interest income grew 4% to S$1.1 billion.
Part of that came from one-off gains on asset sales, and UOB can’t count on those repeating.
Here’s the thing: wealth is where UOB wants to grow.
So on 4 November, check whether wealth fees are still rising at a double-digit clip and whether loan-related fees have stopped sliding.
What is management betting on?
CEO Wee Ee Cheong sees momentum building across UOB’s ASEAN franchise.
He pointed to wealth income, which rose 16% year on year, and card income, which grew 13%.
UOB’s management wants to unlock the value of its retail franchise, grow its wealth business faster and capture regional trade and investment flows.
The third-quarter results will give investors the next chance to see whether these goals are showing up in wealth fees and card income.
What does this mean for UOB’s dividend?
UOB raised its interim dividend to S$0.88 per share from S$0.85 a year ago, with payment made for 28 August 2026.
A bigger dividend is always welcome.
For payouts to keep climbing, UOB needs profit growth that comes from the business itself, not from lower allowances.
Operating profit before allowances tracks that growth, and it fell 4% in the first half.
We won’t get an answer on
dividends
in the coming quarter, but it will set up what to expect in the final quarter of the year.
Get Smart: Look beneath the bottom line
When a bank reports higher profit, don’t stop at the headline.
Look at operating profit before allowances first.
This figure strips out provisions for bad loans and shows you what the core business actually earns.
In the first half, UOB’s net profit rose while its operating profit before allowances fell.
When the bank reports on 4 November, ask yourself one simple question: is operating profit before allowances growing again?
If the answer is yes, UOB’s margins, loans and wealth fees are pulling their weight.
If not, profit growth still depends on lower allowances, and that is what you’ll want to see change.

title: US stocks inch up even as election, AI risks weigh on outlook
article:
(Nov 3): US stocks were higher after the market opened as Americans headed to the polls on Election Day, with control of both chambers of Congress at stake and investors weighing mounting risks to the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

The S&P 500 Index gained 0.2% while the Nasdaq 100 advanced 0.6% as of 9.33am in New York, clawing back earlier losses. Technology shares attempted a rebound a day after entering a correction.

The election adds another layer of uncertainty to an already fragile market backdrop. Polymarket is pricing roughly a 95% probability of Democrats taking the House of Representatives and about a 77% chance of a Senate victory, pointing to a potential sweep of both chambers. The divergence between opinion polls and prediction-market expectations has drawn fresh attention as investors position for the outcome.

History, however, has generally favoured stocks following midterm elections. Large-cap equities have gained about 15% on a market-cap-weighted basis and 16% on an equal-weighted basis in the six months after midterms since 1982, according to Morgan Stanley. Both measures have advanced roughly 22% over the subsequent year.

“For all the prognostications and reactions to tonight’s results, here’s the key stat to remember: While past performance doesn’t guarantee future results, since 1950, so 76 years, the S&P 500 has never been lower 12 months after a midterm election, and that is the most notable point of all for clients,” said Tom Essaye, founder of The Sevens Report.

To UBS Securities, US stocks may be poised for a year-end rebound as favourable seasonality and low hedge fund positioning set the stage for a potential rally after the midterm elections.

See also: US stock rotation hits AI winners on spending worries

“Hyperscaler earnings clearly did not provide the all-clear investors were hoping for, but getting through the election could be the catalyst that unlocks a year-end squeeze,” Davide Montoni, Americas head of institutional equity derivatives and QIS sales at UBS Securities, wrote in a note to clients.

Still, investor positioning suggests caution is building. Investors added a further US$9.6 billion ($12.3 billion) in net new short positions in S&P 500 futures last week, bringing overall positioning close to neutral, according to Citigroup strategists. Nasdaq futures saw a similar trend. Positioning in Russell 2000 futures improved, driven by short-covering and suggesting investors have become less bearish on US small-cap stocks, Citi strategists led by David Chew said.

Concerns about the sustainability of AI spending are adding to the unease. As tech heavyweights increasingly turn to bond markets to finance their AI investments, some of the world’s largest asset managers are warning that the boom risks are developing into a bubble. Pacific Investment Management Co chief executive officer Emmanuel Roman and Bain Capital chair John Connaughton are among investors flagging the possibility of an eventual downturn following the sector’s rapid expansion, even as Wall Street executives continue to tout its long-term potential.

See also: Tech stocks slide as Alphabet’s record plunge revives AI fears

In single stocks, Apple Inc added to the pressure after its latest quarterly results disappointed on several key metrics, including revenue in China. Yum! Brands Inc shares rose as RBC says Taco Bell’s third quarter comparable sales drop of 4% is better than the buyside feared. Palantir Technologies Inc shares tumbled after the software company issued a quarterly outlook that pointed to a potential slowdown in sales growth.

The earnings backdrop has remained relatively resilient. Companies representing about 70% of the S&P 500’s market capitalisation have reported third-quarter results, with 84% beating earnings estimates and 13% missing expectations.
• AI-linked stocks are rebounding after three days of declines. Neocloud firms including CoreWeave and Nebius and chipmaker Intel all gained after the market opened.
• Defence stocks could face another headwind from increased Democratic influence as elections could reset the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 budget towards 2026 levels and flatten spending growth through 2028.
• Energy stocks fell after oil sharply dropped more than 1.7% premarket. Oil-sensitive sectors including travel and cruises are in focus.

title: Binance loses market share to crypto exchange rivals after hack
article:
(Nov 3): Binance may have digested the largest ever crypto hack with relative ease, but not without ceding some of its dominance in digital-asset trading to rivals.

The exchange’s share of crypto trading fell to its lowest level in at least 12 weeks as platforms including OKX gained ground in the aftermath of last week’s US$6.3 billion ($8.1 billion) hack, according to data from Kaiko, an analytics firm.

Over the past seven days, Binance accounted for about 42% of the spot trading volume on the market’s top-10 platforms, down from around 48% prior to the hack and from roughly 51% in mid-August. Coinbase, OKX and Kraken all increased their share in that time.

Binance suspended withdrawals after an Oct 29 cyber-theft that the US Federal Bureau of Investigation has attributed to North Korean hackers — a charge the country denies. Elliptic, the blockchain analytics firm, said its analysis “supports the FBI’s attribution specifically to the North Korean state-linked group TraderTraitor”.

As of Monday, Binance held US$157 billion in assets, a spokesperson said at the time, citing internal estimates that factor in the impact of hack, subsequent withdrawals and price fluctuations. The company had earlier said it had US$171 billion in assets, in an X post on Sunday.

See also: North Korea’s hackers supercharge crypto heists with AI skills

The platform restored withdrawals on Sunday. Customers have since pulled a net US$5.6 billion, about 3.5% of Binance’s total assets, according to a spokesperson.

Now the immediate pressure from the hack appears to be easing. “By around 3:00 UTC on Nov 3, hourly deposits began exceeding hourly withdrawals, reflecting improving user activity and a normalisation of flows,” the spokesperson said.

Fuelled by higher spot trading volume, OKX’s market share rose to about 14% in the past seven days, up from about 11% the prior week, while Coinbase’s grew to 9.6% from about 9%, the Kaiko data show.

title: iX Biopharma says Orion Speciality Labs’ lack of state licence is ‘expected’ at current stage
article:
The board of directors for iX Biopharma confirms that Orion Speciality Lab (Orion) has not yet obtained the licence from the Nevada State Board of Pharmacy.

In the Nov 3 response to SGX’s queries, the company mentioned that this is expected at the current stage, as the licence follows a set of sequence.

“The joint venture between Orion and iX Biopharma first needs to be in place before presenting to the Nevada State Board of Pharamancy. Also, production equipment needs to be installed and be ready for inspection,” the company clarifies.

iX Biopharma mentioned that once these are in place, both parties can submit a manufacturing plan with supporting documents to the Board for review, followed by an inspection of the facility.

“The timing of the Nevada licence is therefore in line with our plans,” the company confirms.

With regards to the Oct 20 article from Politico stating that Orion’s licence application has been tabled on two occasions, iX Biopharma clarifies that any prior application was made by Orion itself.

See also: Sats contractors under MOM probe for false occupation and salary declaration of foreign workers

iX Biopharma adds that the contract with the US Department of Defense (DoD) for the development of Wafermine, awarded in February, is not tied to Orion's site.

“For Wafermine’s supply under the EUA, we are evaluating a number of manufacturing pathways, of which Orion’s site is an option,” the company says.

Meanwhile, iX Biopharma explained its Nov 10, 2025 announcement mentioning that Orion had “operationally ready infrastructure and regulatory licences” means that with Orion being a registered 503B outsourcing facility, meant that the company will not need to build its own US facility from the ground up.

See also: LBD Engineering GM charged with operating dormitory without licence, to step down as subsidiary Metrocon's chairman

“Operationally ready infrastructure referred to Orion's site having the infrastructure ready to host our manufacturing while Regulatory licences referred to Orion's registration with the FDA as a 503B outsourcing facility, which Orion held at the time of the announcement and still holds,” the company states.

Finally, iX Biopharma confirms that there has been no change in joint venture negotiations since the AGM on Oct 16 and both parties are at an advanced stage of negotiations on the final terms and have been carrying out due diligence and tax assessments.

Shares of iX Biopharma closed 3 cents lower, or down 5.88% at 48 cents on Nov 3.

title: Pfizer raises 2026 forecast, extending pharma windfall
article:
(Nov 3): Pfizer Inc raised its full-year outlook after it outperformed in the third quarter, as growing demand for its newer medicines helped the drugmaker offset declining sales of its Covid-19 products.

The drugmaker now expects full-year revenue of US$62 billion to US$64 billion and adjusted earnings of US$2.95 to US$3.05 a share. It previously forecast revenue of US$60.5 billion to US$62.5 billion and adjusted earnings of US$2.80 to US$3 a share.

The New York-based drugmaker reported better-than-anticipated third-quarter profit and sales. It’s the latest pharma company to surpass Wall Street expectations during the period. Last week, Eli Lilly & Co, Merck & Co and Bristol Myers Squibb Co were all among companies that raised their annual forecast.

Shares rose less than 1% in early trading in New York on Tuesday. They’ve gained 23% so far this year, through Monday’s close.

Pfizer is trying to reinvent itself after a major pandemic windfall. CEO Albert Bourla has turned to acquisitions, new cancer medicines and an ambitious push into obesity treatments to revive growth as Covid-19 sales fade and some of the company’s biggest drugs face competition from cheaper alternatives.

One of Pfizer’s major bets is in obesity, where it is seeking to challenge market leaders Eli Lilly & Co and Novo Nordisk A/S. Pfizer bought Metsera Inc last year, gaining experimental treatments including a shot designed to be taken once a month rather than weekly. The company is now advancing an extensive clinical programme to test whether its medicines can compete in the rapidly expanding market.

See also: Neuralink’s China rival targets obesity with ‘electronic’ GLP-1

Cancer is another major focus. Pfizer’s US$43 billion acquisition of Seagen gave it a portfolio of cancer medicines, including Padcev, a treatment for bladder cancer. Sales of that drug beat estimates in the third quarter.

Sales of heart drug Vyndaqel were US$1.77 billion, slightly higher than estimates. Revenues from pneumococcal vaccine Prevnar were US$1.56 billion while the blood thinner Eliquis brought in US$2.52 billion in the quarter.

Pfizer is also seeking to improve profitability through aggressive cost cutting. Separately, the company said Tuesday interim chief financial officer Cecile Guegan would take on the role permanently.

title: Audi and Mercedes hit by walkouts in union push for higher wages
article:
(Nov 3): German metalworkers are stepping up nationwide stoppages as labour officials pursue wage increases and stronger job protections, escalating a dispute affecting about 3.7 million employees.

Companies including Volkswagen AG’s Audi unit, Mercedes-Benz Group AG and Schaeffler AG were hit by walkouts on Monday and Tuesday after a mandatory truce period expired at the end of October.

Germany’s IG Metall union is demanding a 5% wage increase over 12 months and measures to protect jobs and production sites. As part of the latest round of negotiations, employers have offered a one-time payment in 2027 equivalent to 1% of annual gross pay and a 1.3% wage increase effective in July 2028.

The talks come at a particularly challenging time for Germany’s car industry. Automakers are seeking to cut costs as they contend with weak demand in China and heightened domestic competition. Suppliers are also suffering, with Schaeffler AG announcing Tuesday it plans to close five sites in Europe and eliminate 3,460 jobs, some three-quarters of those in Germany.

More significant staffing reductions will be unavoidable, employer representatives warned during the latest negotiating round, unless Germany can substantially reduce hourly labour costs. A third round of talks is due to begin on Thursday, according to IG Metall.

Tensions are especially acute at Ingolstadt-based Audi, where workers grappling with the rising cost of living, particularly prices for energy and fuel, joined a brief stoppage last night.

See also: Tesla Cybercab cruises into Singapore

CEO Gernot Döllner has faced criticism after appearing last month at a campaign event with US President Donald Trump. While Döllner announced plans for Audi’s first US factory at the rally, unions have called for long-term guarantees for German sites.

title: CSE Global secures $434.9 mil new orders in 3QFY2026, up nearly 200% y-o-y
